blocks.text: And in the Talmudic tractate Cholin, fol. 65, where some locusts are said to have גבחת gabbachath and others not to have it, there are those who understand a hump standing out on the back in the manner of a camel; among them is Baal Aruch. But for others גבחת is baldness, as the word is taken in other passages of the Talmud. Accordingly the marginal Gloss explains these Talmudic words about locusts, שאין לו גבחת, One that has no Gabbachath, thus: שאין ראשו מרוט, whose head is not bare. That is, in the Glossator's view, some locusts have a bare head, others a hairy one. Perhaps John alludes to this in Apoc. IX, 8., when he attributes to those mystical locusts τρίχας ὡς τρίχας γυναικῶν [trichas hōs trichas gynaikōn], hair like the hair of women ^{(4)}. Nor do I refer to anything else the fact that the Arabs [III, 274] call a kind of bruchus عرفان [ʿirfān] orphan, as if the name were formed from عرف [ʿurf] orph, that is, from a mane. Alcamus: العرفان جندب ضخم كالجرادة لا يكون الا في رمث او عنظوانة او دويبة صغيرة تكون برمل عالج او الدهنا [al-ʿirfān jundub ḍakhm ka-l-jarāda lā yakūnu illā fī rimth aw ʿunẓuwāna aw duwaybba ṣaghīra takūnu bi-raml ʿālij aw al-dahnā] Alorphan, a kind of bruchus as thick as a locust, usually found nowhere but in ramthsa and onduana (very sour plants, from eating which the belly of camels often swells). Or a small creature living in the sands of Aligi and Dahna: these are places near Medina. I add that in the same Alcamus الخنتف [al-khuntuf] alchanthapho is the name given to الجراد المنتف المنقي للطبخ [al-jarād al-muntaf al-munaqqā li-l-ṭabkh], a locust that is plucked and cleaned for cooking. This is the true explanation, since one who plucks his beard is also called الخنتوف [al-khuntūf] Alchanthouph. From this it plainly follows that some locusts are shaggy and hairy, which our interpreters had not known. Moreover, ילק סמר does not necessarily mean a locust ὀρθότριχα [orthotricha], since we bristle not only with our hair but with our whole body. For hair is not in question when David says, סמר מפחדך בשרי, My flesh bristled for fear of thee. So even a hairless locust can bristle: as when, struck with dread of an approaching enemy and fear of danger, it prepares [col. 457] to defend itself ^{(5)}. And the Prophet, in the passage we are dealing with, could compare horsemen about to fall upon Babylon in great numbers with locusts and bruchi in such a state, against whose invasion it is difficult [III, 275] to defend oneself, as we shall show below. The passage reads: Appoint a commander against her. Bring up horses like bristling locusts: both in number and in their design of laying waste and destroying everything. What if the verbal noun סמר samar, which occurs nowhere else, means not so much bristling as horrifying, striking horror into anyone who sees it? This will fit a swarm of locusts exceedingly well, at whose onset ירגזון כל יושבי ארץ, all the inhabitants of the land tremble, Ioel. II, 1. Hence Hesychius, from some poet, as I suspect: Βρέττανα φοβερὰ [brettana phobera], a horrible locust.

Now we shall say what the ancients thought about this word, so that no one may tire himself in vain consulting them along with me. The Greeks, whom the Arab follows, have for כילק סמר ὡς ἀκρίδων πλῆθος [hōs akridōn plēthos], like a multitude of locusts, as if they had read ספר or מספר for סמר ^{(6)}. Why the Chaldee has for ילק סמר זחלא דמצלהב, a gleaming or shining bruchus, no one could easily say. For gleam and shine have nothing in common with bristling and ὀρθοτριχίᾳ [orthotrichia]. Am I mistaken, or did he too read differently here, namely סגור for סמר, words very close in script? Now סגור is gold, Iob. XXVIII, 15. and throughout 1 Regum and 2 Paralipomenων. So ילק סגור would be a golden bruchus or golden locust, that is, of golden colour and shining like gold: such are the Arabian ones, of which Aelian, Historia book 10, ch. 13: Χρυσοειδῆ οὖν ἰνδάλματα καὶ ἐπ' αὐτῶν κατέστικται [Chrysoeidē oun indalmata kai ep' autōn katestiktai], They are marked with gold-coloured figures. And this very kind of locust could be called by the Chaldee מצלהב, shining, or, with one letter fewer, מצהב, gleaming with golden colour. If it is read so, this conjecture will be firmer. Jerome rendered like a spiny bruchus: with these words the holy man expressed neither the Hebrew adequately nor the nature of the thing. For bruchi or locusts are not distinguished by any stings, unless those mystical ones are meant, to which John attributes the stings of a scorpion, Apoc. IX, 10.^{(7)}. The Syriac has only ܐܝܟ ܩܡܨܐ, like a bruchus, omitting the following word סמר altogether, [III, 276] whether he did not read it or did not understand it. The Hebrews all render like a bruchus with bristling hair. But none of them explains why the bruchus is so called.
